Report Errors in the PDF - support@affairscloud.com Copyright 2014-2026 @ AffairsCloud.com 4 Economic Survey Economic Survey 2025 - 2026 Introduction Every year, an outline of the plans for economic growth is released by the government in the form of the Union Budget. It is an essential policy document that gives an idea about the economic activities to be held in the country along with the government's estimated receipts and expenditures. But to plan out the activities for the current year, it is important to analyze the outcomes of the activities of the previous year. This is where the Economic Survey is used as a tool to assess the previous year's performance. Overview of the Economic Survey 2025-26 On 29th January 2026, the Union Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, Ministry of Finance (MoF) and Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MoCA) presented the Economic Survey 2025-26 in Parliament ahead of the Union Budget for the financial year 2026–27 (FY 27). What is an Economic Survey? The Economic Survey is published every year and reviews the performance of the economy during the previous year. The first economic survey was presented in 1950-51. • The Economic Survey provides a comprehensive view of India’s current economic condition and outlines the government’s assessment of future priorities and challenges. • It sets the context for the Union Budget by highlighting important trends and focus areas for the year ahead. Preparation of the Economic Survey: It is prepared by the Department of Economic Affairs (DEA), under the guidance of Chief Economic Advisor (CEA) to the Government of India (GoI) Venkatramanan Anantha Nageswaran, MoF. • Key inputs and guidance from senior officials in the Ministries of Finance, Revenue, Expenditure, Department of Economic Affairs, DIPAM, and Financial Services were considered. • Contributions were also received from experts, industry bodies, public institutions, and private sector organizations, including regulators and authorities such as Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), Reserve Bank of India (RBI), Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI), International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA), Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA), Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI). • It is presented in both Houses of Parliament by the Union Minister for Finance. About Economic Survey 2025-26: i.This edition of the Economic Survey is longer than earlier editions and includes 17 chapters, reflecting the major changes taking place around the world. ii.The Survey has also updated its base year, shifting it from 2011–12 to 2022–23, to better reflect current economic conditions. iii.The Survey also includes special sections on three long-term themes: Artificial Intelligence (AI), quality of life in Indian cities, and the role of the state and private sector (including households) in building national strength and resilience.

# Page 5^page=5
Report Errors in the PDF - support@affairscloud.com Copyright 2014-2026 @ AffairsCloud.com 5 Economic Survey Highlights of the Economic Survey 2025-26: 1.State of The Economy: Pushing The Growth Frontier i.As per the First Advance Estimates (FAE) by the National Statistical Office (NSO), Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation (MoSPI) India’s real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is expected to grow by 7.4% and Gross Value Added (GVA) by 7.3% in FY26. ii.The country’s potential growth is around 7%, and real GDP growth for FY27 is projected between 6.8% and 7.2%, showing strong growth despite global challenges. iii.According to the FAE, the share of Final Private Consumption Expenditure (PFCE) in GDP increased to 61.5% in the FY26, the highest level since FY 12. This trend is supported by strong consumption growth. 2.Fiscal Developments: Maintaining Stability through Careful Management i.The Centre’s revenue collection has improved over time, rising to around 9.2% of GDP in FY25.Tax collections remained strong, with direct taxes reaching nearly 53% of the budget target by November 2025. ii.Goods and Services Tax (GST) collections also remained strong, reaching Rs 17.4 lakh crore during April–December 2025. iii.On the spending side, capital expenditure (CE) reached about 60% of the budgeted amount by November 2025, while revenue expenditure (RE) growth stayed under control. 3.Monetary Management and Financial Intermediation: Refining the Regulatory Touch In FY26 (April–December 2025), India’s monetary and financial system remained stable and strong, with financial inclusion expanding as over 55 crore bank accounts were opened under the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) by March 2025. • The Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana (PMMY) supports small and micro businesses by providing easy access to credit, with total loan disbursements crossing Rs 36 lakh crore by October 2025. Banking sector i.Banks showed clear improvement in loan quality. The Economic Survey 2025–26 highlights a clear improvement in the health of Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs). By September 2025, bad loans reduced to very low levels, with Gross Non-Performing Assets (GNPA) at 2.2% and Net Non- Performing Assets (NNPA) at 0.5%. ii.Banks have also maintained strong capital strength, with the capital-to-risk-weighted-asset ratio (CRAR) at 17.2% as of September 2025. iii.Bank lending also grew faster, rising to 14.5% by December 2025, compared to 11.2% a year earlier. Capital Markets i.Financial market participation expanded during FY26, with over 235 lakhs new dematerialised (Demat) accounts added by December 2025, taking the total beyond 21.6 crore. ii.Gujarat International Finance Tec-City (GIFT City) is developing as India’s first International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) to attract global capital. 4.External Sector: Playing the Long Game Exports Growth i.Total exports reached a record USD 825.3 billion (bn) in FY25, led by strong growth in services exports.

# Page 6^page=6
Report Errors in the PDF - support@affairscloud.com Copyright 2014-2026 @ AffairsCloud.com 6 Economic Survey ii.Non-petroleum exports reached USD 374.3 bn, with non-petroleum and non-gems exports forming a large share of merchandise exports. Services exports crossed USD 387 bn in FY25. Current Account and Remittances i.The current account deficit (CAD) remained under control, in Q2 FY26, the CAD was around 1.3% of GDP, supported by strong services exports and remittance inflows. ii.India remained the world’s top recipient of remittances, receiving USD 135.4 bn in FY25, supported by higher inflows from skilled Indian workers in advanced economies. Foreign Exchange Reserves India’s foreign exchange reserves stood at USD 701.4 bn as of 16 January 2026, strengthening the country’s ability to withstand global economic shocks. Foreign Investment i.India attracted strong foreign direct investment (FDI), with gross FDI inflows reaching USD 64.7 bn from April to November 2025. ii.In 2024, India was fourth in the world for new Greenfield investment projects, with more than 1,000 initiatives announced. 5.Inflation: Tamed and Anchored i.India recorded its lowest average inflation since the start of the Consumer Price Index (CPI) series, with headline inflation at 1.7 % from April to December 2025, mainly due to declining food and fuel prices. • India saw one of the steepest declines in inflation in 2025, dropping by about 1.8 percentage points from 2024. ii.The International Monetary Fund (IMF) projects inflation at 2.8% for the FY 26 and 4% for FY 27, while the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) expects headline inflation of 3.9% and 4% for the first and second quarters (Q1 & Q2) of FY 27, respectively. 6.Agriculture and Food Management: Raising Productivity, Securing Income and Ensuring Food Security i.The Survey states that agriculture and related sectors are expected to grow by 3.1 % in FY26. Over the last five years, the agriculture and allied sector recorded an average yearly growth of about 4.4 %. • Due to the favourable monsoon, agricultural GVA increased by 3.6 %, compared to 2.7 % in the first half of FY25. However, this growth remains below the long-term average of 4.5 %. • India’s average annual growth rate (AAGR) in agricultural GVA improved significantly, increasing from 3.01 % during 2006–2015 to 4.42 % in the 2015–2024 period. ii.In the Agriculture Year 2024–25, India’s foodgrain production is estimated at 3,577.3 lakh metric tonnes (LMT), up by 254.3 LMT compared to the previous year. iii.Allied sectors such as livestock and fisheries showed steady performance, recording growth of around 5 to 6 %. • Between FY15 and FY24, the livestock sector grew rapidly, with its GVA increasing by almost three times. Fish production also rose by over 140 % between 2014 and 2024. 7.Services: From Stability to New Frontiers: The services sector contributes more than half of India’s GVA. In the first half of FY26, services GVA increased by 9.3 %, with full-year growth expected around 9.1 %.

# Page 7^page=7
Report Errors in the PDF - support@affairscloud.com Copyright 2014-2026 @ AffairsCloud.com 7 Economic Survey • The sector’s share in GDP rose to 53.6 % and its share in GVA reached a record 56.4 % in FY26. All major sub-sectors recorded growth of 8 to 9.9 %. Exports and Global Presence i.India has become the seventh-largest services exporter in the world, with its share in global services trade rising from 2% in 2005 to 4.3% in 2024. Services exports reached an all-time high of USD 387.5 bn in FY25, growing 13.6% YoY. ii.The sector also attracted a major share of FDI, accounting for 80.2% of total FDI during FY23–FY25. • IT (Information Technology) and IT-enabled services (IT-ITES) remain a key driver, with revenues of USD 283 bn (bn) in FY25. • India launched 393 foreign satellites for 34 countries between 2015 and 2024, earning about USD 433 million (mn). Point to Note: Total exports, including merchandise and services, reached a record USD 825.3 bn in FY25, growing 6.1% year-on-year (YoY). India’s share in global merchandise exports increased from 1% in 2005 to 1.8% in 2024 Investment and Employment i.Service sector attracted 80.2 % of total FDI during FY23–FY25, up from 77.7 % in FY16–FY20. ii.The services sector is a key source of jobs, providing 61.9% of urban and formal employment. Tourism sector alone created 8.46 crore jobs in FY24, around 13.3% of total employment. 8.Industry’s Next Leap: Structural Transformation and Global Integration i.Industrial growth in FY26 stayed strong, with Industry GVA rising 7.0% in H1, while manufacturing recovered faster, growing 7.72% in Q1 and 9.13% in Q2. ii.The Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes across 14 sectors attracted over Rs 2.0 lakh crore in investments, resulting in incremental production and sales exceeding Rs 18.7 lakh crore. iii.India’s innovation capacity has improved steadily, with the Global Innovation Index ranking rising to 38th in 2025. India also strengthened its global industrial position, becoming the second-largest producer of steel and cement and the third-largest in pharmaceuticals worldwide. iv.Under the India Semiconductor Mission, 10 semiconductor manufacturing and packaging projects were approved across six states, involving a total investment of around Rs 1.60 lakh crore. 9.Investment and Infrastructure: Strengthening Connectivity, Capacity and Competitiveness Government Investment and Infrastructure Growth i.Government capital expenditure rose to Rs 11.21 lakh crore in FY26, with effective spending reaching Rs 15.48 lakh crore. ii.The national highway network grew 60% to 1,46,572 kilometre (km), high-speed corridors rose ten-fold to 5,364 km, railways reached 69,439 km with 99.1% electrification, and airports expanded to 164 in 2025, making India the third-largest domestic aviation market. iii.The Economic Survey highlights that, as per the World Bank (WB), India ranks among the top five countries worldwide for private investment in infrastructure among low- and middle-income nations. • In South Asia, India leads in private infrastructure investment, receiving more than 90% of the region’s total. Power, Telecom, and Rural Development i.The power sector’s installed capacity rose to 509.74 GW (gigawatt), with Distribution Companies (DISCOMs) posting a Profit After Tax (PAT) of Rs 2,701 crore and Aggregate Technical & Commercial (AT&C) losses falling to 15.04%.

# Page 8^page=8
Report Errors in the PDF - support@affairscloud.com Copyright 2014-2026 @ AffairsCloud.com 8 Economic Survey ii.Renewable Energy (RE) now makes up 49.83% of total capacity. Tele-density reached 86.76%, 5G (fifth generation) covers 99.9% of districts, and over 81% of rural households have clean tap water under the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM). Space Infrastructure India’s space sector strengthened, becoming the fourth nation to achieve autonomous satellite docking (SpaDeX), while expanding domestic missions and boosting connectivity. 10.Environment and Climate Change: Building a Resilient, Competitive and Development- Driven India By 31st December 2025, India added a total of 38.61 GW of RE capacity. This includes 30.16 GW of solar power, 4.47 GW of wind power, 0.03 GW of bio-power, and 3.24 GW of hydroelectric power, marking steady progress in clean energy expansion. 11.Education and Health: What Works and What’s Next i.The Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) in India stands at 90.9% in primary, 90.3% in upper primary, 78.7% in secondary, and 58.4% in higher secondary. ii.Higher education has expanded to 70,018 institutions by June 2025, two international IIT (Indian Institute of Technology) campuses in Zanzibar (Tanzania) and Abu Dhabi (United Arab Emirates, UAE). • Under the National Education Policy (NEP), 170 universities have adopted the National Credit Framework (NCrF), iii.In health, India has reduced Maternal Mortality Rate (MMR) by 86%, under-five mortality (U5MR) by 78%, neonatal mortality (NMR) by 70%, and infant mortality rate (IMR) by over 37% in the last decade, showing major progress in healthcare outcomes. 12.Employment and Skill Development: Getting Skilling Right i.According to the Economic Survey, the Labour Codes address key challenges such as income volatility and benefit gaps, by formally recognising gig and platform workers They aim to strengthen worker welfare, improve business flexibility, and could contribute around 1.25% to India’s GDP by FY 30. ii.The e-Shram portal has registered over 31 crore unorganised workers by January 2026, with women making up more than 54% of registrants. In Q2 FY26, India had 56.2 crore people employed aged 15 and above. iii.In the skill development sector, the National Scheme for Upgradation of Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) aims to modernise 1,000 government ITIs—200 hubs and 800 spokes—through smart classrooms and industry-aligned courses. 13.Rural Development and Social Progress: From Participation to Partnerships i.India’s poverty rates in 2022-23 were 5.3% for extreme poverty and 23.9% for lower-middle- income poverty, according to the revised international poverty line. Government spending on social services has been rising steadily, reaching 7.9% of GDP in FY26. ii.In rural areas, the SVAMITVA scheme has completed drone surveys in 3.28 lakh villages (target: 3.44 lakh), with 2.76 crore property cards prepared across 1.82 lakh villages.

Report Errors in the PDF - support@affairscloud.com Copyright 2014-2026 @ AffairsCloud.com 9 Economic Survey 14.Evolution of the AI Ecosystem in India: The Way Forward India’s Artificial Intelligence (AI) ecosystem is expanding through small, task-specific models in healthcare, agriculture, education, urban planning, disaster management, and public administration, working on local hardware with low resources to solve real-world problems. 15.Urbanisation: Making India’s Cities Work for its Citizens The Namo Bharat Regional Rapid Transit System demonstrates how fast regional transport can transform cities and nearby towns. By reducing travel times, it makes jobs more accessible, supports the growth of multiple urban centres, and eases crowding in major cities. 16.From Import Substitution to Strategic Resilience and Indispensability India’s ‘Swadeshi’ strategy now focuses on critical, high-benefit, and cost-effective sectors. • By cutting input costs and boosting domestic capabilities, the country is shifting from mere import replacement to building global strategic strength, making “buying Indian” seamless.
